related_questions.question: How long do long COVID headaches last?
related_questions.snippet: Like other COVID symptoms, such as a fever, coughing, and a sore throat, COVID headaches usually clear up in a few days. One study found that COVID headaches typically lasted 4 days. But sometimes, a COVID headache can last for months after your other symptoms go away and you no longer test positive for COVID.
related_questions.title: COVID Headache: How Long Does It Last? - WebMD

related_questions.question: What causes a headache that won't go away?

text_blocks.snippet: A headache that won't go away can stem from various causes, including migraines, head injuries, or underlying conditions like meningitis or a stroke. It could also be due to medication overuse or structural problems in the head, neck, or spine. If a headache persists for days and doesn't respond to over-the-counter pain relievers, it's crucial to seek medical advice.
snippet_highlighted_words: migraines, head injuries, or underlying conditions like meningitis or a stroke

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at potential causes:

list.title: Migraines:
list.snippet: These can cause severe, throbbing pain, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound.

list.title: Tension Headaches:
list.snippet: These headaches can feel like a tight band around the head and are often triggered by stress, fatigue, or poor posture.

list.title: Head Injuries:
list.snippet: Even minor head injuries, like a concussion, can lead to prolonged headaches.

list.title: Medication Overuse Headaches:
list.snippet: Frequent use of pain relievers for headaches can sometimes lead to rebound headaches when the medication wears off.

list.title: Structural Problems:
list.snippet: Conditions like arthritis or malformations in the spine or neck can cause cervicogenic headaches, where pain originates in the neck and radiates to the head.

list.title: Meningitis:
list.snippet: Inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord can cause severe headaches along with fever and stiff neck.

list.title: Stroke:
list.snippet: A sudden, severe headache can be a symptom of a stroke.

list.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia:
list.snippet: This condition involves irritation of a nerve in the face, causing intense, sharp, and stabbing pain.

list.title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage:
list.snippet: Bleeding in the space around the brain can cause a sudden, severe headache.
Headaches lasting for days: If over-the-counter medications don't provide relief, consult a doctor.
Headaches accompanied by fever, stiff neck, vision changes, confusion, or seizures: These could indicate a serious underlying condition.
Headaches that worsen over time: This could signal a progression of a condition or the development of a new problem.
Headaches that interfere with daily activities: If headaches are significantly impacting your ability to work, study, or enjoy life, seek professional help.

related_questions.question: What does a stroke headache feel like?

text_blocks.snippet: A stroke headache can feel like a very severe headache that comes on suddenly and intensely, sometimes described as a "thunderclap" headache. It may be accompanied by other stroke symptoms like weakness, numbness, dizziness, or speech difficulties. The location and severity of the headache can vary depending on the type and location of the stroke.
snippet_highlighted_words: a very severe headache that comes on suddenly and intensely, sometimes described as a "thunderclap" headache

list.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke (bleeding in the brain):
list.snippet: Often associated with a "thunderclap headache," which is a sudden, intense headache that reaches its peak severity within seconds or minutes. It may be localized to one side of the head or affect the entire head.

list.title: Ischemic Stroke (blockage in a blood vessel):
list.snippet: May cause a headache with a tension-type headache quality, described as a dull, aching pain and pressure, sometimes affecting one or both sides of the head.

list.title: Location:
list.snippet: The location of the headache can be related to the area of the brain affected by the stroke. For example, a stroke in the carotid artery (which supplies blood to the front of the brain) might cause a headache in the forehead, while a stroke in the vertebrobasilar system (which supplies blood to the back of the brain) might trigger a headache at the top of the neck.

list.title: Severity:
list.snippet: Stroke headaches are often severe and may be accompanied by other symptoms like nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light and sound, or even aura symptoms (like visual disturbances or numbness).

list.title: Warning Signs:
list.snippet: Some strokes may be preceded by a "sentinel headache," which is a less severe headache that can be a warning sign of an impending aneurysm rupture.

text_blocks.snippet: Important Note: Any sudden and severe headache, especially if accompanied by other stroke symptoms, should be evaluated by a medical professional immediately, as prompt treatment is crucial for stroke.

related_questions.question: What is the best painkiller for headaches?

text_blocks.snippet: For most headaches, over-the-counter medications like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) are effective choices as they reduce inflammation. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) can also be helpful, but some find ibuprofen more effective. For migraines, triptans (like sumatriptan) are often prescribed and are more effective than over-the-counter options.

list.title: Ibuprofen:
list.snippet: This NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) is effective for many types of headaches, including migraines, and works by reducing inflammation.

list.title: Naproxen:
list.snippet: Another NSAID, naproxen (Aleve) provides longer-lasting pain relief than ibuprofen.

list.title: Acetaminophen:
list.snippet: This pain reliever is a good option for mild to moderate headaches, but some find it less effective than ibuprofen for migraines.

list.title: Aspirin:
list.snippet: Aspirin can also be effective for headaches and is an NSAID.

list.title: Excedrin:
list.snippet: This combination medication containing aspirin, acetaminophen, and caffeine can be effective for some, but its effectiveness varies.

list.title: Triptans:
list.snippet: These are a class of drugs specifically designed for migraines and are generally more effective than over-the-counter options. Examples include sumatriptan (Imitrex) and eletriptan (Relpax).

list.title: Ergots:
list.snippet: Another class of drugs used for migraines, though they are generally considered less effective than triptans.

text_blocks.snippet: Tips for choosing and using pain relievers:

list.snippet: Start early: Take medication as soon as you feel a headache coming on.
Follow directions: Do not exceed the recommended dosage on the packaging.
Consider other factors: If you have stomach issues, NSAIDs may not be the best choice. If you have kidney problems, acetaminophen may be a safer option.
Lifestyle changes: Along with medication, consider other factors that may be contributing to your headaches, such as stress, dehydration, or lack of sleep.
If your headaches are severe, frequent, or don't respond to over-the-counter medications, consult with your doctor.
If you experience other symptoms along with your headache, such as fever, stiff neck, vision changes, or confusion, seek immediate medical attention.
